t.kizil cave temple complex@41.8,82.5:
Kizil is a Turkic word meaning red, and the name suits the landscape around these caves, where bare ridges of rust-coloured rock stand over the Muzat river on the northern edge of the Taklamakan Desert. Between about the third and eighth centuries, Buddhist monks cut hundreds of caves into a sandstone cliff here, some as cells to live and meditate in, some as halls with a central pillar around which pilgrims could walk, and covered the walls with murals. This was the kingdom of Kucha, a rich oasis state on the northern Silk Road, and its artists blended Indian, Persian and Chinese styles into something distinctive.

The murals are the point. They show scenes from the lives of the Buddha, legends of earlier lives, musicians, dancers and celestial beings, painted with minerals imported from far away, including lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, whose deep blue glows in some caves. Kucha was the birthplace of Kumarajiva, a monk and scholar who in the late fourth century was carried away to China and translated Buddhist scriptures into Chinese, shaping the religion for centuries. The caves suffered badly over time, from natural decay, from iconoclasm and in the early twentieth century from European expeditions, which cut murals out of the walls and shipped them to Berlin, where many were later destroyed in the Second World War. What remains is partial, but still beautiful.

The riding in Xinjiang is on a grand scale. The highway south of the Tian Shan range runs through enormous distances, with snow peaks to the north and bare desert to the south, and traffic is thin. A famous road crosses the Tian Shan north of Kuqa, with long climbs and tight bends through gorges of red rock, though it is closed for months each winter. Wind and dust are common, and summers are hot, with winter nights very cold. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Kuqa, a town of nearly seventy thousand, lies thirty-six kilometres away by the data and has fuel, restaurants and hotels. Services thin out quickly outside, so take fuel and water whenever you pass a station. Foreign visitors to Xinjiang are subject to checkpoints and permits, so carry your passport and check the current situation before you plan a ride. Lamb kebabs, flatbread and sweet melons are the local food, and the grape arbours in the villages offer welcome shade.
t.nalati@43.4,84.0:
Nalati, known in Kazakh as Narat, is a high grassland on the northern slopes of the Tian Shan in Xinjiang, in the far west of China, and it is one of those landscapes that looks like a painter's idea of mountain summer pasture. Rolling green meadows spread beneath snowy peaks, dotted with spruce forest and herders' yurts, and the air is cool and thin at around two thousand metres. The Kazakh herders who move their sheep, horses and cattle up here every summer are the people who made the grasslands what they are.

The Duku Highway, which runs from Dushanzi in the north to Kuqa in the south, is one of the most spectacular roads in China, and Nalati is on its northern half. The highway crosses the Tian Shan, in places through deep gorges and over high passes, and is known for its changes of scenery, from green meadows through canyons of red rock to desert in the south. It is the kind of road that closes in winter because of snow and avalanches, and is usually open only from about early summer to autumn, so check before you go.

The Ili valley below, to the west, is Xinjiang's fruit-growing heartland, famous for apples and apricots, and the wild apple forests that grow in the foothills are thought to be related to the ancestors of the cultivated apple. Yining, the main city, is a few hours away. This is a region of many peoples, with Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Han Chinese, Hui and others, and the food is correspondingly varied: lamb on skewers, hand-pulled noodles, flatbread from tandoor ovens and strong tea with milk.

Riding in China as a foreigner is complicated: it generally requires local licensing, a registered vehicle and often a guide, and checkpoints are common in Xinjiang, so this is a route that needs advance planning. Fuel is available in towns but can be far apart on remote sections, so I would not trust the gauge. Weather changes quickly in the mountains, with cold rain and even snow in summer. The meadows are at their greenest in June and July, and early mornings are cold.
t.bayinbuluke@43.0,84.2:
Bayinbuluke is a vast, high grassland basin in the Tian Shan of Xinjiang, around two and a half thousand metres up, and the second largest grassland in China. The Kaidu River winds across it in great loops, and in evening light it looks like a silver snake draped over an emerald carpet. The Torghut Mongols graze their sheep and horses here, and herds of yaks and cattle dot the slopes. The pin marks the end of the Duku Highway's best-known section, where the road finally leaves the mountains and wanders out into the open.

The Duku Highway, which runs from Dushanzi in the north to Kuqa in the south, is one of the great mountain roads of China. It crosses the Tian Shan range over passes above three thousand metres, with hairpins, snow sheds, canyons and wide plateaus. This part, around Bayinbuluke, is smooth and fast, and the road is wide, but weather changes fast. Cold wind, rain, even snow can arrive on a summer afternoon, and the road is closed in winter, usually from around November until spring, so check the dates carefully.

Bayinbuluke also hosts a swan reserve, home to whooper swans and other birds that nest in the marshes in summer. The nine bends of the Kaidu River, seen from a viewing platform, are one of the region's iconic sights, and sunrise and sunset are the best times to see them. Mongol yurts are scattered across the plain, and some offer tea and basic food to visitors.

A reminder for riders: as in the rest of China, foreigners cannot simply ride here with their own bikes, and you will need a licensed operator and the right permits. Fuel and food are available in Bayinbuluke town and in the larger centres on either side, but distances are long, and services are sparse between. Carry water, warm clothing and a good map, because phone signal can disappear for hours at a time.
t.hashilegen pass@43.4,84.5:
Hashilegen Pass lies high in the central Tian Shan at roughly 3,400 metres, where the Duku Highway climbs to the divide and the world turns to rock, snow and sky. The scenery is wide and austere, with glaciers on the high peaks, meltwater streams across the alpine meadows and the occasional herder's felt tent. The pin sits at the top, a place where it is easy to feel small.

The road is a serious mountain crossing. It climbs in long bends and hairpins, steeply in places, and the air thins quickly as you rise. Wind, cold and sudden changes in the weather are normal, and snow can fall in any month. The surface is mostly good, but potholes and rock falls are common, especially after storms. The pass is closed in winter, from about November, and reopens only after the heavy snow has been cleared in spring, so the ride season is short and the road is at its best in summer and early autumn.

The Tian Shan, which means Celestial Mountains in Chinese, stretch for thousands of kilometres across Central Asia, and their glaciers feed the rivers that water the deserts of Xinjiang. The region is home to Kazakh, Mongol, Uyghur and Han communities, each with their own food, music and traditions, and the pastoral life of the highland herders is a living tradition. In summer you will see flocks of sheep and herds of horses moving up to the high pastures, and the grass is dotted with wild flowers.

Services are almost non-existent at the pass, so bring water and food, extra layers and a fully fuelled bike. Phone signal is patchy, and the nearest towns are far away. The mountain light is sharp and bright, and the sunsets can be spectacular, but do not linger too late, as temperatures drop quickly after dark. Foreign riders should note that China requires special permits and licensed guides for foreign motorcyclists.
t.kizilgaha beacon tower@41.8,82.9:
The Silk Road did not take a single line across Central Asia, it split around the Taklamakan desert, and along its northern branch, under the snow peaks of the Tian Shan, lay a chain of oasis towns. Kuqa was one of the biggest, the old kingdom of Kucha, a centre of Buddhism, music and dance, and the home of the monk Kumarajiva, who translated Buddhist texts into Chinese. Kizilgaha, a few kilometres from the town, holds one of the beacon towers that the Han and Tang dynasties built to signal across the desert, a squat tower of rammed earth, about the height of a three-storey house, standing on a rise over a dry plain.

The towers worked by smoke and fire. A guard on duty would light a signal, by day with smoke, by night with flame, and the next tower in line would repeat it, sending news of raiders or armies hundreds of kilometres in a short time. Some towers stand alone and others were part of a fortified post, with barracks and storehouses. The ground around is bare, pale and cracked, and the air is dry and hot in summer, but the red mountains of the Kizil cave temples lie nearby, with their painted caves of Buddhas and musicians. Together these sites are part of a World Heritage listing for the Silk Roads.

Riding in this part of Xinjiang is vast and dramatic. The roads are broad and well surfaced, running past cotton fields, poplar lines and open desert, with the Tian Shan on the northern horizon, and the Tarim Basin to the south. Distances are great, and fuel stations are spaced out, so it pays to fill the tank when you can. Heat in July and August is fierce, with sandstorms from the Taklamakan, and winter is bitterly cold. Spring and autumn are the best times. Foreign riders face strict rules in China, with permits, checkpoints and restrictions in Xinjiang, so check the current position before planning.

Kuqa, about nine kilometres away, is a city of some seventy thousand, with fuel, markets, a Sunday bazaar, and restaurants serving lamb kebabs, hand-pulled noodles and the local naan, pita-like bread baked in clay ovens. Sweet apricots and grapes in summer are worth buying from stalls by the road. The old town has a mosque and a few traditional houses. Carry water and sun protection, and dress conservatively. Carry your passport at all times for checkpoints.
t.subash buddhist ruins@41.9,83.1:
The Tarim Basin is a very large, very dry bowl, and Kuqa sits on its northern rim where the Tian Shan drops its meltwater onto the plain. Subash, about eighteen kilometres north of town, is what remains of a Buddhist monastery that once straddled the Kuqa river, with one half of the complex on each bank. The river is a gravel-and-mud braid for most of the year, and the ruins around it are the colour of the ground: mud-brick stupas, walls and cell blocks that have been eroded into soft shapes by centuries of wind and the occasional flood.

In its day this was a big deal. Kucha, as the old kingdom was called, was one of the great oases of the northern Silk Road, a place where Indian, Iranian and Chinese influences met, and where monks translated sutras and musicians developed a style that later reached the courts of Tang China. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang passed through in the seventh century and wrote about the monasteries here, including the pair on opposite banks of the river. Standing among the foundations you can read that history in the layout without needing a plaque to tell you.

The riding is the kind that suits this part of Xinjiang. The roads out of Kuqa are wide and straight, bordered by poplar windbreaks and cotton or jujube fields, then they climb gently toward bare brown foothills. The corners are few, the horizons long, and the main enemy is the sun and the wind that can blow dust across the carriageway in the afternoon. Start early. The light on the hills is best in the first hours, and it gets properly hot by midday in summer.

The same ride links Subash with the Kizil cave-temples and the Kizilgaha beacon tower, which is a good way to see how the Buddhist and military sides of the Silk Road shared the same corridor. Kuqa itself has the fuel, the food and the beds, and since it is a town of nearly seventy thousand people you will not struggle to find a meal. Grilled lamb, flatbread baked in a tandoor-style oven and fresh melon are the sensible choices on this side of the country. Carry water to the ruins, because there is very little shade out there and nowhere to buy a bottle once you leave the road.

Allow time to walk rather than ride the last bit. The site rewards slow looking, and the silence, broken only by wind and the occasional bird, is part of why it is worth the detour.
t.dushanzi@44.3,84.9:
Dushanzi is where the desert gives way to the mountains in northern Xinjiang, a city of oil refineries and chemical plants at the foot of the Tian Shan, and its main interest to riders is that it is the northern end of the Duku Highway. That road climbs south across the range, passing through snowy summits, high grasslands and canyons, before dropping into the Tarim Basin at Kuqa, a journey of roughly five hundred and fifty kilometres through some of the most dramatic scenery in China.

The town itself is blunt and industrial, with wide boulevards and steel towers, and has little to offer except fuel, food and a bed. It is, however, a good place to prepare. The land north of the mountains is flat and dry, the Junggar Basin stretching toward the horizon, and the Tian Shan appears as a white wall in the distance on a clear day. Dust and haze are common, and the wind can be fierce.

South of the city, the highway enters the Dushanzi Grand Canyon, a gorge of striped red and ochre rock carved by a river, and the road follows it in a series of tight bends. Beyond that lies Kuitun and then the high pastures of the Narat and Bayanbulak regions, grasslands where Kazakh and Mongol herders move their sheep and horses in summer. At Bayanbulak, the wide marshy plain is a breeding ground for swans, and the road crosses a high pass with a view of glaciers. The route finishes with the red canyons of Kuqa, one of the largest canyon landscapes in the country.

The Duku Highway is a seasonal road, snowbound for much of the year, and it generally opens in early summer and closes again in autumn. Check conditions locally, because landslides and snow can shut it without notice, and sections may be limited by weather or construction. The road surface is generally good, but altitude, long climbs and sudden weather changes demand attention.

Fuel is important. Fill up in Dushanzi and at every opportunity on the way, because the stations are far apart and some may be closed. Carry cash, food and warm clothes, and be prepared for checkpoints where identity papers and vehicle documents may be examined. Foreign visitors should check permit requirements before departure.
t.kuqa@41.7,83.0:
Kuqa lies on the northern rim of the Taklamakan Desert, in Xinjiang, at the southern foot of the Tian Shan, and it has been a stop on the Silk Road for two thousand years. Known in Chinese chronicles as Kucha, it was the capital of an oasis kingdom that grew rich on trade and became a major centre of Buddhism in the first millennium. Its musicians and dancers were famous across Asia, and the monk Kumarajiva, born here in the fourth century, became one of the great translators of Buddhist texts into Chinese. Today the Uyghur town has a rebuilt old quarter, a big mosque, a Sunday market and a good deal of melons, apricots and grapes.

The great monuments lie outside town. The Kizil Caves, about sixty-five kilometres to the west, are a set of Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff above a dry river, decorated with murals that include blue, green and white pigments from lapis lazuli, and that are among the earliest Buddhist paintings in China. Closer to town, the ruined city of Subashi and the Kumtura caves reward those with time to spare. The landscape is stark: yellow earth, red cliffs and scattered poplars, with the pale line of the Tian Shan to the north.

The Duku Highway, which ends here, is one of the great mountain roads of China. It crosses the Tian Shan from the green meadows around Nalati, high in the range, through snowy passes and deep canyons, and descends in a long run to the desert oasis at Kuqa, passing red rock gorges and glacier-fed streams. The road is usually closed by snow from about November until spring, and landslides and rockfalls can block it at any time, so check conditions locally. Fuel stations are sparse in the mountains, so fill up before you leave Nalati or at the larger towns, and be ready for checkpoints and ID inspections that are common in the region.

I should say plainly that foreign visitors cannot normally ride their own motorcycles in China without special permits, a Chinese driving licence and a licensed guide, so this is a route to plan well in advance with a specialist, if at all.

Kuqa has about sixty-eight thousand people in the urban area, with plenty of services. Try the lamb kebabs, the flat bread called nang, and the sweet local apricots in summer.
